claim: Loss-of-function mutations in MECP2 cause Rett syndrome.
source: Loss-of-function mutations in MECP2 (human gene) cause a severe childhood disorder called Rett syndrome (Amir et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amir et al., 1999

claim: Rett syndrome patients experience motor deterioration that manifests as ataxia, apraxia, hypotonia, and spasticity.
source: Of these symptoms, motor deterioration is a significant problem for patients and manifests as ataxia, apraxia, hypotonia, and spasticity (Neul et al., 2014; Sandweiss et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Neul et al., 2014 and Sandweiss et al., 2020

claim: Complete loss of Mecp2 in mice causes deficits in motor coordination and motor learning, hind limb clasping, hypoactivity, and tremors.
source: In mice, the complete loss of Mecp2 (mouse gene) causes deficits in motor coordination and motor learning, hind limb clasping, hypoactivity, and tremors that mimic those seen in patients (Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001; Pelka et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001; Guy et al., 2001; Pelka et al., 2006

claim: Mice that conditionally lack Mecp2 in the cortex or basal ganglia partially replicate Rett-like motor impairments.
source: Furthermore, mice that conditionally lack Mecp2 in the cortex or basal ganglia partially replicate these Rett-like impairments (Chen et al., 2001; Gemelli et al., 2006; Su et al., 2015), suggesting that forebrain dysfunction contributes to the motor deficits seen in patients.
evidence: Supported by citations to Chen et al., 2001; Gemelli et al., 2006; Su et al., 2015

claim: The cerebellum contains approximately 75% of all neurons in the brain.
source: The cerebellum contains approximately 75% of all neurons in the brain (Lange, 1975; Sarko et al., 2009) and integrates sensory inputs in order to fine-tune motor output (Manto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lange, 1975 and Sarko et al., 2009

claim: The cerebellum integrates sensory inputs to fine-tune motor output.
source: The cerebellum contains approximately 75% of all neurons in the brain (Lange, 1975; Sarko et al., 2009) and integrates sensory inputs in order to fine-tune motor output (Manto et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manto et al., 2012

claim: Impairments in cerebellar circuitry cause ataxia, dystonia, and tremor.
source: This function is critical for motor coordination and motor learning as impairments in the cerebellar circuitry cause ataxia, dystonia, and tremor (White et al., 2016; Bostan and Strick, 2018; Darmohray et al., 2019; Machado et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to White et al., 2016; Bostan and Strick, 2018; Darmohray et al., 2019; Machado et al., 2020

claim: The cerebellum contributes to non-motor behaviors such as social interaction, reward, and memory.
source: The cerebellum also contributes to non-motor behaviors such as social interaction, reward, and memory (Wagner et al., 2017; Carta et al., 2019; McAfee et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wagner et al., 2017; Carta et al., 2019; McAfee et al., 2019; Kelly et al., 2020

claim: MeCP2 is expressed in granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons in the cerebellum.
source: MeCP2 was expressed in granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons (Figure 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A-D

claim: Deleting Mecp2 from the cerebellum using En1Cre causes a delay in motor learning in 6-month-old mice.
source: Although the performance of 2- and 4-month-old cerebellar KO mice was normal compared to control mice, 6-month-old cerebellar KO mice had an initial motor learning delay that was overcome with additional training (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by rotarod behavioral data shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B

claim: The motor learning delay in cerebellar KO mice is overcome with additional training.
source: Although the performance of 2- and 4-month-old cerebellar KO mice was normal compared to control mice, 6-month-old cerebellar KO mice had an initial motor learning delay that was overcome with additional training (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by rotarod behavioral data showing improvement over training days in Figure 2A,B

claim: Motor learning deficits in cerebellar KO mice are not due to abnormalities in general locomotor activity or strength.
source: These motor learning deficits were not due to abnormalities in general locomotor activity or strength (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C–F showing no differences in locomotor activity or strength measures

claim: Cerebellar KO mice do not have deficits in sensorimotor gating, social behavior, or contextual fear memory.
source: Although the cerebellum is implicated in non-motor behaviors (Klein et al., 2016), we did not observe any deficits in sensorimotor gating, social behavior, or contextual fear memory in cerebellar KO mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3G–K).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3G–K showing no differences in these measures

claim: Mice lacking Mecp2 in granule cells (Atoh1Cre), Purkinje cells (Pcp2Cre), or Purkinje cells and molecular layer interneurons (Ptf1aCre) do not show rotarod deficits at 6 months of age.
source: However, we did not detect rotarod deficits in cell type-specific KO animals at an age when cerebellar KO mice were symptomatic (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by rotarod behavioral data in Figure 2C showing no differences in cell type-specific KO mice

claim: Cerebellar KO mice exhibit an initial delay in the probability and amplitude of eyelid closure during eyeblink conditioning that improves with additional training.
source: Compared to control mice, cerebellar KO mice exhibited an initial delay in the probability and amplitude of eyelid closure that improved with additional training, suggesting that cerebellar-dependent motor learning is disrupted by the loss of Mecp2 (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by eyeblink conditioning data in Figure 2E

claim: Simple spike firing is more irregular in cerebellar KO mice, as evidenced by increased coefficient of variation (CV) and coefficient of variation 2 (CV2).
source: Although the mean firing rates were unchanged, simple spike firing was more irregular in cerebellar KO mice, as was evident by an increase in the coefficient of variation (CV) and coefficient of variation 2 (CV2) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3D showing increased CV and CV2

claim: Mean simple spike firing rates are unchanged in cerebellar KO mice.
source: Although the mean firing rates were unchanged, simple spike firing was more irregular in cerebellar KO mice, as was evident by an increase in the coefficient of variation (CV) and coefficient of variation 2 (CV2) (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 3D showing no difference in mean firing rates

claim: Purkinje cell morphology is not affected in cerebellar KO mice.
source: This electrophysiological abnormality was not due to defects in Purkinje cell morphology or the density of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic puncta (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by Golgi staining and Sholl analysis data in Figure 3E showing no differences in morphology

claim: The density of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic puncta is not affected in cerebellar KO mice.
source: This electrophysiological abnormality was not due to defects in Purkinje cell morphology or the density of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic puncta (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: Supported by synaptic puncta density data in Figure 3F showing no differences

claim: H3K9me3 levels in heterochromatic foci are reduced in granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons of cerebellar KO mice (En1Cre).
source: In cerebellar KO mice (En1Cre), the level of H3K9me3 was reduced in the heterochromatic foci of granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons, but the levels of DAPI, H3K4me3, and H3K27me3 were unaffected (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C showing reduced H3K9me3 intensity

claim: DAPI, H3K4me3, and H3K27me3 levels in heterochromatic foci are unaffected in cerebellar KO mice (En1Cre).
source: In cerebellar KO mice (En1Cre), the level of H3K9me3 was reduced in the heterochromatic foci of granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons, but the levels of DAPI, H3K4me3, and H3K27me3 were unaffected (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4A, B, and D showing no differences

claim: H3K9me3 levels in heterochromatic foci are reduced in granule cells of Atoh1Cre KO mice.
source: Interestingly, this phenomenon was also observed in granule cells of Atoh1Cre KO mice, Purkinje cells of Pcp2Cre KO mice, and Purkinje cells and molecular layer interneurons of Ptf1aCre KO mice (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C

claim: H3K9me3 levels in heterochromatic foci are reduced in Purkinje cells of Pcp2Cre KO mice.
source: Interestingly, this phenomenon was also observed in granule cells of Atoh1Cre KO mice, Purkinje cells of Pcp2Cre KO mice, and Purkinje cells and molecular layer interneurons of Ptf1aCre KO mice (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C

claim: H3K9me3 levels in heterochromatic foci are reduced in Purkinje cells and molecular layer interneurons of Ptf1aCre KO mice.
source: Interestingly, this phenomenon was also observed in granule cells of Atoh1Cre KO mice, Purkinje cells of Pcp2Cre KO mice, and Purkinje cells and molecular layer interneurons of Ptf1aCre KO mice (Figure 4A–D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 4C

claim: Changes in heterochromatic foci are present in cell type-specific KO mice that lack behavioral phenotypes.
source: It is noteworthy that this change was present in mice lacking Mecp2 in neuronal subtypes of the cerebellum, even though these mice lacked behavioral phenotypes (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by comparison of heterochromatin data in Figure 4 with behavioral data in Figure 2C

claim: Non-motor phenotypes in Rett syndrome are likely not caused by cerebellar dysfunction.
source: First, we did not observe non-motor phenotypes in cerebellar KO mice even though the cerebellum is implicated in non-motor behaviors such as social interaction and cognition (Mauk et al., 2000; Tsai et al., 2012; Klein et al., 2016). This suggests that non-motor phenotypes in Rett syndrome are likely not caused by cerebellar dysfunction.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of non-motor phenotypes in cerebellar KO mice despite cerebellar involvement in non-motor behaviors

claim: Cerebellar-related motor deficits result from combined dysfunction in the entire circuit rather than dysfunction in a single cell type.
source: Second, we did not observe motor deficits in any of the cell type-specific KO mice. The same phenomenon is seen for the sensorimotor gating deficits of Mecp2 null mice, which are present in mice lacking Mecp2 in all inhibitory neurons but not in individual subtypes of inhibitory neurons (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015). This suggests that the cerebellar-related motor deficits are the result of combined dysfunction in the entire circuit rather than dysfunction in a single cell type.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of motor deficits in En1Cre KO mice but not in cell type-specific KO mice, supported by citations to Chao et al., 2010 and Ito-Ishida et al., 2015

claim: Behavioral deficits in cerebellar KO mice are milder than in mice lacking Mecp2 in the cortex and basal ganglia.
source: Finally, the behavioral deficits in cerebellar KO mice were milder than mice lacking Mecp2 in the cortex and basal ganglia. In cerebellar KO mice, the phenotypes were restricted to motor learning and appeared in 6-month-old mice, whereas the motor deficits in mice lacking Mecp2 in the cortex and basal ganglia are more profound and arise in 2-month-old mice (Chen et al., 2001; Gemelli et al., 2006; Su et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by comparison of behavioral data with cited studies (Chen et al., 2001; Gemelli et al., 2006; Su et al., 2015)

claim: Motor symptoms of Rett syndrome arise from a combination of cerebellar, cortical, and basal ganglia dysfunction.
source: Thus, the motor symptoms of Rett syndrome arise from a combination of cerebellar, cortical, and basal ganglia dysfunction.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of phenotypes across different brain region-specific KO mice

claim: Purkinje cells serve as the final output stage of the cerebellar cortex and integrate synaptic inputs from granule cells, molecular layer interneurons, and inferior olivary neurons.
source: Purkinje cells serve as the final output stage of the cerebellar cortex and integrate synaptic inputs from granule cells, molecular layer interneurons, and inferior olivary neurons (Arancillo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arancillo et al., 2015

claim: Purkinje cells are an ideal cell type for determining if functional defects occurred at any point in the cerebellar circuit.
source: Thus, they are an ideal cell type for determining if functional defects occurred at any point in the cerebellar circuit.
evidence: Inferred from the role of Purkinje cells as the final output stage integrating multiple inputs

claim: Irregular firing rates of Purkinje cells suggest that motor phenotypes of KO mice are caused by defects in the cerebellar circuitry.
source: The irregular firing rates of Purkinje cells suggest that the motor phenotypes of KO mice are caused by defects in the cerebellar circuitry.
evidence: Inferred from the electrophysiological data showing irregular Purkinje cell firing

claim: Loss of the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ pump in mice causes motor incoordination and dystonia.
source: For example, the loss of the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ pump in mice causes motor incoordination and dystonia (Calderon et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Calderon et al., 2011

claim: In mice lacking the α3 isoform of the Na+/K+ pump, the mean firing rate of Purkinje cells is normal, but the firing rates are irregular.
source: In these mice, the mean firing rate of their Purkinje cells is normal, but the firing rates are irregular, similar to what we observed in cerebellar KO mice (Fremont et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fremont et al., 2014

claim: Purkinje cells of Car8wdl mice have irregular simple spike activity, which contributes to motor incoordination on the rotarod.
source: Just like cerebellar KO mice, the Purkinje cells of Car8wdl mice have irregular simple spike activity, which ultimately contributes to motor incoordination on the rotarod (White et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 2016

claim: Irregularity of simple spike firing could arise from impairments in intrinsic Purkinje cell responses, abnormal excitatory input from granule cells, and/or perturbations in synaptic modulation from molecular layer interneurons.
source: Because Purkinje cells integrate input from multiple cell types, the irregularity of simple spike firing could arise from a combination of factors including impairments in intrinsic Purkinje cell responses, abnormal excitatory input from granule cells, and/or perturbations in synaptic modulation from molecular layer interneurons.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms underlying the observed irregular firing

claim: Changes in heterochromatic foci of Mecp2-null hippocampal neurons are present in presymptomatic Mecp2+/− female mice.
source: Similar to our findings, changes in the heterochromatic foci of Mecp2-null hippocampal neurons are present in presymptomatic Mecp2+/– female mice (Ito-Ishida et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito-Ishida et al., 2020

claim: In symptomatic Mecp2+/− female mice, the levels of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, but not H3K9me3, are elevated in Mecp2-null hippocampal neurons.
source: In symptomatic Mecp2+/− female mice, the levels of H3K4me3 and H3K27me3, but not H3K9me3, were elevated in Mecp2-null hippocampal neurons (Ito-Ishida et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ito-Ishida et al., 2020

claim: H4K20me3 is abnormally distributed in Mecp2-null hippocampal neurons, but not cerebellar granule neurons.
source: In addition, H4K20me3 is abnormally distributed in Mecp2-null hippocampal neurons, but not cerebellar granule neurons (Linhoff et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Linhoff et al., 2015

claim: Alterations in heterochromatin architecture do not always coincide with behavioral abnormalities.
source: Thus, our results indicate that alterations in heterochromatin architecture do not always coincide with behavioral abnormalities and are influenced by the particular cell type and histone modification.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cell type-specific KO mice show heterochromatin changes but lack behavioral phenotypes

claim: Alterations in heterochromatin architecture are influenced by the particular cell type and histone modification.
source: Thus, our results indicate that alterations in heterochromatin architecture do not always coincide with behavioral abnormalities and are influenced by the particular cell type and histone modification.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of different histone modifications across different cell types and brain regions

claim: En1Cre is expressed in the midbrain, spinal cord interneurons, and muscle.
source: En1Cre is expressed in the midbrain, spinal cord interneurons, and muscle (Atit et al., 2006; Joyner and Zervas, 2006; Bikoff et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Atit et al., 2006; Joyner and Zervas, 2006; Bikoff et al., 2016

claim: Removing Mecp2 from dopaminergic neurons does not affect rotarod performance.
source: First, removing Mecp2 from dopaminergic neurons, including those in the midbrain, does not affect rotarod performance (Samaco et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Samaco et al., 2009

claim: Eyeblink conditioning is mediated by circuits in the cerebellum and brainstem.
source: Second, although the loss of Mecp2 in spinal cord interneurons could contribute to defects on the rotarod, it is unlikely to affect eyeblink conditioning as this reflex is mediated by circuits in the cerebellum and brainstem (Bracha, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bracha, 2004

claim: Loss of Mecp2 in skeletal muscle does not affect muscle morphology or physiology.
source: Third, the loss of Mecp2 in skeletal muscle does not affect muscle morphology or physiology (Conti et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conti et al., 2015

claim: Ptf1aCre is expressed in inferior olivary neurons.
source: Moreover, Ptf1aCre is expressed in inferior olivary neurons, a main source of input to the cerebellum (Hoshino et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hoshino et al., 2005

claim: Loss of Mecp2 in inferior olivary neurons does not disrupt motor function in mice.
source: The absence of motor phenotypes in Ptf1aCre KO mice suggests that the loss of Mecp2 in inferior olivary neurons does not disrupt motor function in mice.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of motor phenotypes in Ptf1aCre KO mice

claim: Improvement in motor learning after additional training in cerebellar KO mice is not observed in other Mecp2 KO mice.
source: A unique and interesting finding was the improvement in motor learning after additional training in cerebellar KO mice. To our knowledge, this phenomenon is not observed in other Mecp2 KO mice (Li and Pozzo-Miller, 2012; Lombardi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li and Pozzo-Miller, 2012 and Lombardi et al., 2015

claim: Memory deficits in female Mecp2 heterozygous mice are rescued with forniceal deep brain stimulation (DBS).
source: However, a related effect is seen in female Mecp2 heterozygous mice in which their memory deficits are rescued with forniceal deep brain stimulation (DBS) (Hao et al., 2015; Lu et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hao et al., 2015 and Lu et al., 2016

claim: The effects of DBS on brain circuitry share similarities to that of repetitive activation during training.
source: The effects of DBS on brain circuitry share similarities to that of repetitive activation during training (De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015; Herrington et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Langille and Brown, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Zeeuw and Ten Brinke, 2015; Herrington et al., 2016; Lu et al., 2016; Langille and Brown, 2018

claim: Activation of the cerebellar circuitry during training may improve motor phenotypes in cerebellar KO mice by enhancing synaptic function.
source: In cerebellar KO mice, it is possible that activation of the cerebellar circuitry during training improves their motor phenotypes by enhancing synaptic function in a manner similar to the proposed mechanism of DBS.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms underlying the observed improvement with training

claim: Repetitive circuit activation via training could improve other behavioral deficits in Mecp2 KO mice.
source: This also raises the possibility that repetitive circuit activation via training could improve other behavioral deficits in Mecp2 KO mice.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential therapeutic implications

claim: Cerebellar dysfunction contributes to motor deficits following the loss of Mecp2.
source: Taken together, our results reveal that cerebellar dysfunction contributes to motor deficits following the loss of Mecp2.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral and electrophysiological data presented in the study

claim: Behavioral, synaptic, and cellular deficits in cerebellar KO mice are relatively mild compared to other Mecp2 KO models.
source: Interestingly, the behavioral, synaptic, and cellular deficits in cerebellar KO mice were relatively mild compared to other Mecp2 KO models.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of the current study's findings with cited literature on other Mecp2 KO models

claim: Neuronal subtypes between brain regions, and even those within a brain region, respond differently to the loss of Mecp2.
source: So, even though Mecp2 is broadly expressed throughout the brain, neuronal subtypes between brain regions, and even those within a brain region, respond differently to the loss of Mecp2.
evidence: Inferred from the differential phenotypes observed across different brain region-specific and cell type-specific KO mice

claim: The functional consequences of Mecp2 loss are context specific.
source: As future studies seek to better define the function of Mecp2 and use this knowledge to design effective therapies, it is important to keep in mind that the functional consequences of Mecp2 loss are context specific.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that different cell types and brain regions show different responses to Mecp2 loss

claim: Deleting Mecp2 from the cerebellum causes irregular firing rates of Purkinje cells.
source: We observed irregular firing rates of Purkinje cells and altered heterochromatin architecture within the cerebellum of knockout mice.
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data presented in the manuscript

claim: Deleting Mecp2 from the cerebellum causes altered heterochromatin architecture.
source: We observed irregular firing rates of Purkinje cells and altered heterochromatin architecture within the cerebellum of knockout mice.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data on histone modifications presented in the manuscript

claim: Motor deficits present in Rett syndrome arise, in part, from cerebellar dysfunction.
source: These findings demonstrate that the motor deficits present in Rett syndrome arise, in part, from cerebellar dysfunction.
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral and electrophysiological findings in cerebellar KO mice

claim: Rett syndrome patients lose previously acquired milestones after a period of normal development.
source: After a period of normal development, patients lose previously acquired milestones and develop debilitating neurological deficits (Hagberg et al., 1983; Neul et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hagberg et al., 1983 and Neul et al., 2014

claim: Removing Mecp2 perturbs synaptic function in cortical and hippocampal neurons.
source: Because removing Mecp2 perturbs synaptic function in cortical and hippocampal neurons (Na et al., 2013; He et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2016; Ure et al., 2016), we hypothesized that alterations in the electrophysiological properties of cerebellar neurons might explain the motor phenotypes in cerebellar KO mice.
evidence: Supported by citations to Na et al., 2013; He et al., 2014; Meng et al., 2016; Ure et al., 2016

claim: MeCP2 regulates heterochromatin structure in cortical and hippocampal neurons.
source: Multiple studies have demonstrated that MeCP2 regulates heterochromatin structure in cortical and hippocampal neurons (Baker et al., 2013; Linhoff et al., 2015; Ito-Ishida et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Baker et al., 2013; Linhoff et al., 2015; Ito-Ishida et al., 2020

claim: Distinct behavioral phenotypes arise when Mecp2 is removed from different subtypes of inhibitory neurons.
source: Furthermore, distinct behavioral phenotypes arise when Mecp2 is removed from different subtypes of inhibitory neurons (Ito-Ishida et al., 2015; Mossner et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ito-Ishida et al., 2015 and Mossner et al., 2020

claim: Altered social behavior in Mecp2 KO mice originates from dysfunction of parvalbumin-expressing inhibitory neurons.
source: For example, altered social behavior and seizures in Mecp2 KO mice originate from dysfunction o parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons, respectively (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2010 and Ito-Ishida et al., 2015

claim: Seizures in Mecp2 KO mice originate from dysfunction of somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons.
source: For example, altered social behavior and seizures in Mecp2 KO mice originate from dysfunction o parvalbumin- and somatostatin-expressing inhibitory neurons, respectively (Chao et al., 2010; Ito-Ishida et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2010 and Ito-Ishida et al., 2015

claim: Multiple brain regions including the cortex and basal ganglia contribute to motor learning on the rotarod.
source: In addition to the cerebellum, multiple brain regions including the cortex and basal ganglia contribute to motor learning on the rotarod (Sakayori et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sakayori et al., 2019

claim: The cerebellum is strictly necessary for eyeblink conditioning.
source: Therefore, we used eyeblink conditioning, an alternate task of motor learning for which the cerebellum is strictly necessary, to validate the motor learning deficits observed in cerebellar KO mice (Figure 2D; Heiney et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Heiney et al., 2014

claim: Purkinje cells in lobule V are largely zebrin negative.
source: Focusing on lobule V instead of widely sampling from the cerebellum allowed us to compare the results of Purkinje cells within the same cerebellar subregion while minimizing the effect of zebrin-derived differences in firing proprieties because Purkinje cells in lobule V are largely zebrin negative (Ozol et al., 1999; Zhou et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ozol et al., 1999; Zhou et al., 2014; Peter et al., 2016

claim: Simple spikes originate from granule cell inputs to Purkinje cells.
source: To accomplish this, we monitored the activity of Purkinje cells in awake animals by recording their simple spikes, which originate from granule cell inputs, and complex spikes, which originate from inferior olivary neuron inputs (Schmolesky et al., 2002; Davie et al., 2008; Arancillo et al., 2015; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmolesky et al., 2002; Davie et al., 2008; Arancillo et al., 2015

claim: Complex spikes originate from inferior olivary neuron inputs to Purkinje cells.
source: To accomplish this, we monitored the activity of Purkinje cells in awake animals by recording their simple spikes, which originate from granule cell inputs, and complex spikes, which originate from inferior olivary neuron inputs (Schmolesky et al., 2002; Davie et al., 2008; Arancillo et al., 2015; Figure 3A–C).
evidence: Supported by citations to Schmolesky et al., 2002; Davie et al., 2008; Arancillo et al., 2015

claim: Purkinje cells serve as a reliable indicator of circuit dysfunction in the cerebellar circuit.
source: Because Purkinje cells are the final output stage of the cerebellar cortex, they serve as a reliable indicator of circuit dysfunction in the cerebellar circuit (Arancillo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Arancillo et al., 2015

claim: The ventral portion of lobule V includes the cerebellar microzone that supports eyeblink conditioning.
source: We targeted Purkinje cells at the ventral portion of lobule V, targeting cells in the medial wall of the primary fissure, which includes the cerebellar microzone that supports eyeblink conditioning (Heiney et al., 2014; Ohmae and Medina, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Heiney et al., 2014 and Ohmae and Medina, 2015

claim: MeCP2 is a nuclear protein that binds methylated cytosines on DNA throughout the genome and regulates gene expression.
source: MeCP2 is a nuclear protein that binds methylated cytosines on DNA throughout the genome and regulates gene expression (Tillotson and Bird, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Tillotson and Bird, 2019

claim: Behavioral deficits originate from dysfunction in excitatory and inhibitory neurons in other Mecp2 KO mice.
source: Studies from other Mecp2 KO mice have demonstrated that behavioral deficits originate from dysfunction in excitatory and inhibitory neurons (Chao et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chao et al., 2010 and Meng et al., 2016

claim: Synaptic changes in cerebellar KO mice are mild compared to those observed in other Mecp2 KO models.
source: Although the synaptic changes in cerebellar KO mice were mild compared to those observed in other Mecp2 KO models (Chao et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2016), they may still contribute to the behavioral deficits since similar findings are observed in other mouse models of cerebellar dysfunction.
evidence: Inferred from comparison with cited studies (Chao et al., 2010; Meng et al., 2016)

claim: Healthy mice spend progressively more time on a rotating rod as their motor skill improves in the rotarod assay.
source: In this assay, healthy mice spend progressively more time on a rotating rod as their motor skill improves, while mice with incoordination and motor learning impairments spend less time on the apparatus.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the rotarod assay

claim: Mice with incoordination and motor learning impairments spend less time on the rotarod apparatus.
source: In this assay, healthy mice spend progressively more time on a rotating rod as their motor skill improves, while mice with incoordination and motor learning impairments spend less time on the apparatus.
evidence: Based on established knowledge of the rotarod assay

claim: The cerebellum is involved in motor coordination and learning.
source: Because the cerebellum is involved in motor coordination and learning (Mauk et al., 2000), we analyzed the motor performance of cerebellar KO mice using the rotarod (Deacon, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mauk et al., 2000

claim: 2-month-old cerebellar KO mice have normal rotarod performance compared to control mice.
source: Although the performance of 2- and 4-month-old cerebellar KO mice was normal compared to control mice, 6-month-old cerebellar KO mice had an initial motor learning delay that was overcome with additional training (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by rotarod data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A

claim: 4-month-old cerebellar KO mice have normal rotarod performance compared to control mice.
source: Although the performance of 2- and 4-month-old cerebellar KO mice was normal compared to control mice, 6-month-old cerebellar KO mice had an initial motor learning delay that was overcome with additional training (Figure 2A,B; Figure 2—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by rotarod data in Figure 2—figure supplement 3B

claim: MeCP2 is expressed in approximately 98-99% of NeuN+, Calbindin+, and Parvalbumin+ neurons in the cerebellum.
source: Quantification of the percentage of NeuN+, Calbindin+, and Parvalbumin+ neurons that express MeCP2. N = 4 biologically independent mice per group. Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 1D

claim: MeCP2 protein levels are significantly reduced in the cerebellum but not the hippocampus of En1Cre KO mice.
source: Quantification of MeCP2 protein levels normalized to Histone H3 in the cerebellum and hippocampus of Flox and KO mice.
evidence: Supported by Western blot quantification in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D showing significant reduction in cerebellum (p<0.0001) but not hippocampus (ns)

claim: En1Cre drives recombination in granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons of the cerebellum.
source: We verified the recombination efficiency using Rosa26lsl-tdTomato reporter mice and found that granule cells, Purkinje cells, and molecular layer interneurons expressed tdTomato (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C; Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–B,D–E,G–H).
evidence: Supported by tdTomato reporter expression data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C

claim: Atoh1Cre drives recombination specifically in granule cells.

claim: Loss of Mecp2 in molecular layer interneurons alone does not cause motor deficits.
source: Finally, although Ptf1aCre removes Mecp2 from Purkinje cells and molecular layer interneurons, the absence of motor deficits in Pcp2Cre KO mice, which only targets Purkinje cells, indicates that the loss of Mecp2 from molecular layer interneurons does not cause the behavioral deficits seen in En1Cre KO mice.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of Ptf1aCre and Pcp2Cre KO mice phenotypes
